opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. This is a question I care deeply about, because if you look at the history of AI, data has always been the quiet engine underneath every breakthrough. With ImageNet, we learned that scale and diversity of data can unlock capabilities nobody expected. Embodied AI, robotics especially, doesn't have its ImageNet moment yet, and a big reason is that collecting real-world interaction data is slow, expensive, and frankly limited in diversity. You can only teleoperate a robot in so many kitchens.

Where I think Marble can help is in generating rich, explorable, 3D-consistent worlds. Not just pretty pictures, but spaces with geometry and structure that an agent can move through and reason about. If you can take a text prompt, an image, or a few views and turn that into a coherent environment, you can suddenly create a huge variety of scenes: different layouts, lighting, clutter, materials, styles. That variety is exactly what embodied agents need to generalize instead of overfitting to the three labs they were trained in.

I want to be careful, though. Generated worlds aren't a full replacement for real-world data. Physics, contact, the messiness of real objects: there's still a gap, and the community needs to be honest about it. What I see is complementary. Use generated worlds for breadth and for training perception, navigation, and spatial reasoning at scale, then ground and refine with real-world data. Over time, as these world models become more physically faithful, that balance will shift.

At a deeper level, this connects to what I believe about spatial intelligence. Language models learned from the enormous body of human text. For machines to truly understand and act in the 3D world, they need an equivalent abundance of worlds to learn from. Helping create that abundance is one of the most exciting things we can contribute.

r001.rationale: The response discusses limits of collecting real-world interaction data, but does not identify internet video’s limited controllability.

r002.rationale: It does not identify the effort of constructing simulated environments as a bottleneck.

r003.rationale: It proposes Marble for generating varied, explorable 3D worlds to train embodied agents at scale.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. So, the way I think about it is this: the data problem for embodied AI is fundamentally different from the data problem we solved with ImageNet. With images, the internet had already done the collection for us. We just needed to organize and label it. But there is no internet of physical interaction. Nobody has been uploading trillions of examples of a robot opening a drawer or walking through a cluttered kitchen. And you can't collect that at scale in the real world, because every trial takes real time, real hardware, and sometimes real breakage.

So the question becomes: where does the data come from? And our answer at World Labs is that it has to be generated, but generated from models that actually understand three-dimensional structure. That's what Marble is. It's a world model that takes something very sparse, a text prompt, a single image, a short video, and produces a full, persistent, navigable 3D environment. Not a video that looks right from one viewpoint, but a space you can walk through, where the geometry is consistent, where if you turn around the wall is still where you left it.

That persistence is the whole point for embodied agents. An agent needs to act, observe the consequence, and act again. If the world hallucinates differently every time the camera moves, the agent learns nothing useful. With Marble, you can spawn thousands of varied environments, kitchens with different layouts, warehouses with different clutter, outdoor scenes with different lighting, and each one is a stable place for an agent to explore and fail and try again. You can export them, edit them, compose them, drop them into a simulator with physics.

And I want to be honest about what it does and doesn't solve. Marble gives you visual and spatial diversity at a scale you could never build by hand. What it doesn't fully give you yet is the contact-rich physics, the friction, the deformable objects, the things that make manipulation genuinely hard. That's the next frontier, and we're working toward it. But I think of this the way I thought about ImageNet back then. The first step is getting the breadth of the world into a form a model can learn from. Marble is that step for spatial intelligence. Once the agent has seen a hundred thousand plausible rooms, the sim-to-real gap gets a lot narrower, and the precious real-world data you do collect goes much further.

r001.rationale: The response says there is no internet-scale collection of physical interactions, but it does not identify limited controllability of internet video as a drawback.

r002.rationale: It describes creating environments by hand as something that cannot provide diversity at scale, identifying manual environment construction as a bottleneck.

r003.rationale: It presents Marble as a world model that generates persistent, navigable 3D environments for embodied agents to explore and train in.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that embodied agents need more than images or text. They need experience: acting in a world, seeing what changes, and learning from the consequences. Collecting all of that in the physical world is slow and expensive.

The opportunity with Marble is to help create rich 3D environments where agents can have those experiences across a much wider variety of settings. You can imagine varying the layout of a room or the placement of objects, so an agent learns something more general than how to succeed in one particular scene.

But generating environments is only part of the answer. Those environments also need to support meaningful interactions, and we have to test whether what an agent learns transfers to the real world. I see this as a way to expand and complement real-world training, with physical experience remaining an essential grounding.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the cost of collecting physical-world experience, but does not identify limited controllability of internet video.

r002.rationale: It says physical data collection is slow and expensive and that environment generation is only part of the answer; it does not identify the effort of constructing simulated environments as a bottleneck.

r003.rationale: It proposes using Marble to create rich 3D environments where embodied agents can gain training experience across varied settings.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the opportunity is to move beyond collecting every interaction in the physical world. For embodied agents, data is not just images or text—it’s actions and their consequences. What happens when I move through a space, reach for something, or encounter an obstacle?

A world model could help us generate varied environments where agents can practice those interactions. That’s how I see Marble potentially helping: as a foundation for creating worlds that expand the diversity of training experiences.

But we have to be careful. A world that looks convincing to a human is not necessarily a world with the physical consistency a robot needs. The important question is whether training in those environments produces capabilities that transfer to the real world. So I see this as complementing real-world data, with a lot of work still needed to establish that transfer.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the need for varied embodied-agent experiences, but does not identify internet video or its limited controllability.

r002.rationale: The response does not describe the effort of constructing simulated environments as a bottleneck.

r003.rationale: It presents Marble as a foundation for creating varied worlds where embodied agents can practice interactions, expanding their training experiences.
